1.title: Plotting From The End For A Cozy Mystery

children.text: is often considered the false ending. It's the darkest moment in the book is when the protagonist (our sleuth) loses all hope.
Crisis: The worst has happened. Everything the characters have tried to avoid has come to fruition.
Usually revealed in a single scene, ending with things worse off than anyone realized.
But the story must continue, so the protagonist pulls themselves up,  and then the stakes are raised again as the book moves to its finale, the climax.
The battle is being fought in an all-or-nothing struggle with the ending in still in doubt.
Set the scene, this is important in a cozy to ground the reader into the story.

cards.title: The sleuth takes on the case

children.text: By the end of ACT 1, the sleuth has to decide to take action. She/he cannot be still.
WHY, what's at stake for them if they do nothing?
And why does this person think they can do anything the police can't?
Reveal more about your sleuth, history, conflicts, problems. (Make sure your GMC is built (I have 3 videos on how to do that on You Tube).
Remember your sleuth will move forward, then have to retrace their steps as their ideas DON'T pan out.
A. Reveal facts about suspects, through interrogations and the discovery of clues.
Bring more of your town in, repeating characters you're building for future books that perhaps been accused mistakenly and trust will need to be built again.  Or the opposite.
B. Flight, or disappearance of one or more suspect.
C. Develop a sense of urgency. Raise the stakes or make it evident that if the mystery is not solved soon, there will be terrible consequences.
All of this leads to the midpoint.
Now that the sleuth has rebounded from the Black Moment and creates the climax, hoping it will work...
What kind of reveal do you want?
A room full of suspects that will act as the denouement as the sleuth explains it all and then finger points to the actual killer.

Both? ( I generally use both as in a cozy, the sleuth will need to know the truth from the killer that they were right about him/her being the killer and why, but also we're generally in a first person POV so it needs to be told to the sleuth's cohorts.
To know which is best, be sure you know your sleuth well enough to know they work better one way or the other. Or think they can which could then add complications.
A major plot twist appears. This keeps the story from just being on the same old, same old track.
This twist can put your character back to square one, rethink everything, even question her ability.

This is hard on your character and the reader, after all they're enjoying your book trying to figure who dunnit, and now your sleuth is really struggling. But you as the author must keep the story moving, the character must continue on despite the bad odds of getting whatever their goal is for the story to come to fruition. Justice, Vengeance,  Settling The Score, Acquittal, Trust etc.
This leads us to the Black Moment.

cards.title: My False Ending Act II Break

children.text: This is the event that disrupts the story's peaceful status quo—typically the discovery of a murder—and draws the amateur sleuth into the investigation, whether by personal connection to the victim, suspicion falling on them or someone they love, or dissatisfaction with the official investigation.
Develop the crime and the perpetrator
Know the history of the killer
Create a backstory in detail using GMC for this character.
Make sure they can do the crime!
Once this is established as well as the Denouement, you can go forward to chapter one. But you can't easily write the book unless these last parts is created in detail.
Knowing the motive and the trigger is key to the story working well from page one and will keep you from rewriting numerous times.
Hate crime (usually not in a cozy mystery)
Then develop the emotional reason behind the
Your sleuth's antagonist who could also be their "inside person" will play a big role here.
What is at stake, what changes with the murder?
How, what is the ticking clock for your sleuth?
This is where the reader is going to find out why the killer felt they had to kill the victim. Revenge, payback? The end of the story except for the final moments afterwards. You need to know this!
Generally it's something in the past that has festered in the killers mind, but it really it's up to your story.
Having this established at the beginning allows you to build the story from this first point no fumbling around after the fact. You know. You may change parts of it, but the crux is the same.

Where a suspect says they were when the crime happened. Give it one small flaw the sleuth can later poke holes in.
A moment where new info flips what the reader believed was true. Use it to turn a suspect into an innocent, or an innocent into a suspect.
A sudden change in direction — a friend becomes a suspect, a lead goes cold, or the sleuth's theory falls apart. Use it to keep the middle of the story moving.
A moment where the sleuth (or someone they care about) is put at risk — physically, socially, or otherwise. Use it to raise stakes and remind readers this isn't just a puzzle.
